food.text: Coffeehouses developed first in the Ottoman Empire and then spread to Italy and across Europe. They were lucrative businesses that generated tax revenue and rent.

Fernand Braudel credits the Ottomans with introducing rice, sesame and maize to the region. Ottoman trade brought new ingredients from Asia and the Americas that enriched regional cuisines and gave Ottoman foodways their evolving, unique character.

In Ottoman cuisine, fruit frequently accompanied meat as a side dish. Plums, apricots, pomegranates, pears, apples, grapes, figs and quinces, along with many kinds of citrus, were used fresh or dried.
Ottoman influence on European food began in the early 16th century. Francesco I de'Medici requested a recipe for "Turkish sorbette" in 1577, and sharbat spread first to Italy.

Around the port of Galata, coffeehouses, sharbat shops and bozahanes served imported coffee, sugar and other colonial goods arriving in Istanbul in the 18th century. Bozahanes had been among the most popular public hangouts in 15th- and 16th-century Bursa until the coffeehouses overshadowed them in the 17th century.

The 16th-century Flemish diplomat Ogier Ghiselin de Busbecq called Ottoman culinary culture "very frugal". In his account, a simple meal of bread and salt, garlic or onion and yoghurt was all that was needed for nourishment.

Before the war with the Ottomans, the Mamluks drafted farmers and peasants from rural areas as soldiers, and the men fled to avoid being drafted. The shortage of rural workers needed for food production led to a shortage of bread and a near famine that devastated towns from Cairo to Anatolia.

Coffeehouses developed first in the Ottoman Empire and spread to Italy, then across Europe. In the 18th century, coffeehouses, sharbat shops and bozahanes clustered around the port of Galata, where imported coffee, sugar and other colonial goods arrived in Istanbul.

Rice pudding, described in contemporaneous sources as "Turkish-style rice", was served at the wedding of Ercole I d'Este, Duke of Ferrara, in 1529. Koz halva, similar to nougat, is found in Central Europe, where Hungarians call it Törökméz, meaning 'Turkish honey'.

Lady Mary Wortley Montagu, writing in the 18th century, said Ottomans use "a great deal of rich spice". She grew weary of the intensity of flavors and asked that her own cook add a dish or two in the English manner. A 17th-century report, by contrast, said spice use in Istanbul was moderate and mostly limited to black pepper.

The Ottoman and Mamluk states vied for control of the spice trade after the Ottomans took Constantinople in 1453. Their rivalry led to the Ottoman–Mamluk War of 1516–1517, which brought Cairo, Damascus and Aleppo under Ottoman rule.

Evliya Çelebi, writing in the 17th century, described receiving a plate of wheat soup from the "Table of Abraham" in Hebron. He said he never witnessed such a tasty meal at the table of either viziers or men of learning. In the 16th century the simat still served lentils each day, with pomegranate seeds and seasoned rice on Thursday evenings.

A 17th-century report says the use of spice in Istanbul was moderate and mostly limited to black pepper. Because the intensity of spice is subjective, other reports differ, and that disagreement is part of the historical record.

art.text: The 16th and 17th centuries are generally recognized as the finest period for art in the Ottoman Empire, much of it linked to the imperial court. The long reign of Suleiman the Magnificent, from 1520 to 1566, combined political and military success with strong encouragement of the arts.

The most important architect of the classical Ottoman period was Mimar Sinan. His major works include the Şehzade Mosque, the Süleymaniye Mosque and the Selimiye Mosque, monumental buildings focused around a high central dome with a varying number of semi-domes.

Turkish carpets appear in Western paintings, and documents show that Ottoman-made carpets of the "Transylvanian" type were exported to Europe in large quantities. The increase in production probably reflects rising demand from an upper middle class that could now afford to buy them.

Major Ottoman religious monuments were typically built as a külliye, an architectural complex with several components. These could include a mosque, a madrasa, a hammam, an imaret, a sebil, a market, a caravanserai or a primary school. Early experiments with building types evolved into the classical Ottoman style of the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Bayezid II Mosque in Istanbul was built between 1500 and 1505 under the architect Ya'qub, also called Yakubshah. Its prayer hall uses two semi-domes aligned with the central dome, creating a "cascade of domes" profile likely influenced by the Hagia Sophia.

The tilework of the Rüstem Pasha Mosque (1561–1562) is an exception to Mimar Sinan's usually restrained use of tile decoration. It also marks the beginning of the artistic peak of Iznik ceramic art from the 1560s onward.

Ottoman Baroque architecture emerged in the 1740s during the reign of Mahmud I, influenced by European Baroque. Its most important early monument was the Nuruosmaniye Mosque, completed in 1755, a clear departure from the classical style.

Turkish calligraphy reached the height of its popularity under Suleiman the Magnificent. The Diwani script was distinguished by complex lines within each letter and closely packed letters within each word.

The Bayezid II Mosque in Istanbul was built between 1500 and 1505 under the architect Ya'qub, or Yakubshah. It was part of a larger complex with a madrasa, a hammam, hospices, an imaret, a caravanserai and a cemetery around the sultan's mausoleum. The madrasa now serves as a Museum of Turkish Calligraphy Art.

Iznik tile art used blue colours predominantly, but the important "tomato red" began to appear. Its motifs included tulips, hyacinths, carnations, roses, pomegranates, artichoke leaves, narcissus and Chinese "cloud" motifs.

After Sinan, Davud Agha became chief architect of the classical style, which grew more repetitive. His works in Istanbul include the Koca Sinan Pasha Complex (1593) and the Tomb of Murad III, completed in 1599.

The tughra was an elaborately stylized formal signature of the sultan. Like the hilya, an illuminated sheet of calligraphy describing the prophet Muhammad, it performed some of the functions of portraits in Christian Europe.

The palace workshops, known as the nakkashane, worked in many media but apparently not pottery or textiles. Their craftsmen were apparently a mixture of slaves, trained Turks and foreign specialists. The slaves were especially Persians who had been captured in war, at least in the early periods, and were put to work for the palace as unfree labour.

Cornelis de Vos's 1620 Portrait of Abraham Grapheus is among the earliest paintings to show "Transylvanian" type Ottoman carpets. Pieter de Hooch's 1663 painting Portrait of a family making music depicts an Ottoman prayer rug of the same type.
The second half of the 16th century saw the apogee of certain Ottoman decorative arts. This was most notable in the use of Iznik tiles.

In the 18th century Ottoman architecture became more open to external influences, including Baroque architecture from Western Europe. Changes appeared during the Tulip Period, which was followed by the emergence of the Ottoman Baroque style in the 1740s.

The Bayezid II Mosque has a prayer hall with two semi-domes aligned with the main central dome, while each side aisle is covered by four smaller domes. This creates a sophisticated "cascade of domes" profile, likely reflecting the influence of Hagia Sophia. The mosque is considered the last step towards the classical Ottoman style.

The madrasa of the Bayezid II complex in Istanbul now serves as a Museum of Turkish Calligraphy Art. The complex also included a monumental hammam, hospices, an imaret, a caravanserai and a cemetery around the sultan's mausoleum.

war.text: On 23 August 1514 at the Battle of Chaldiran, the Ottoman Empire won a decisive victory over the Safavid Empire. The Safavids suffered disastrous losses as Ottoman artillery and janissary gunfire cut down their cavalry. As a result, the Ottomans annexed Eastern Anatolia and Upper Mesopotamia from Safavid Iran, marking the first Ottoman expansion into Eastern Anatolia and halting Safavid expansion to the west.

The Ottoman–Persian Wars pitted the Ottoman Empire against the emerging Iranian state of Ismail I of the Safavid dynasty. The two were arch rivals, divided by religion: the Ottomans were staunchly Sunni and the Safavids Shia. For centuries they competed for control over eastern Anatolia, the Caucasus, and Ottoman Iraq.

After the Ottoman–Safavid War (1532–1555), the Caucasus was partitioned between the Safavids and the Ottomans for the first time. Under the Peace of Amasya, Western Armenia, western Kurdistan and Western Georgia went to the Ottomans, while southern Dagestan, Eastern Armenia, Eastern Georgia and Azerbaijan stayed Persian. This status quo lasted until the Russian conquest of the Caucasus in the 19th century.

Shah Abbas I conquered the Ottoman Transcaucasian domains in 1604 and forcibly deported the Armenians of Eastern Armenia to inner Persia. Armenian peasants were resettled in Gilan and Mazandaran, while merchants and artisans were moved near Isfahan. There they formed New Julfa, named after their hometown, Julfa, on the Arax River.

At Chaldiran, the Ottomans fielded a larger, better-equipped army of 60,000 to 100,000 with many heavy artillery pieces and thousands of Janissaries with gunpowder weapons. The Safavid army numbered 40,000 to 80,000 and had no artillery, only traditional weaponry. Its cavalry charged the Ottoman wings, but the highly maneuverable Ottoman cannons and muskets decimated them.

Chaldiran was only the beginning of 41 years of destructive war between the Safavids and Ottomans, which ended in 1555 with the Peace of Amasya. The Safavids eventually reconquered Mesopotamia and Eastern Anatolia under Abbas the Great, who ruled from 1588 to 1629. The 1639 Treaty of Zuhab permanently ceded those lands to the Ottomans.

Among the many Ottoman–Persian treaties, the Treaty of Zuhab of 1639 is usually considered the most significant. It fixed the present borders between Turkey and Iran and between Iraq and Iran. Later treaties frequently referred back to it.

Simeon of Poland travelled across the Ottoman Empire from 1608 to 1618 and recorded the toll of the Celali rebellions on Armenian communities. He noted that half of the Armenian households in Tokat were dispersed or killed. In Sivas, 1,400 of 2,000 Armenian households suffered the same fate.

At Chaldiran, Ismail I, the leader of the Safavids, was wounded and almost captured. The Ottoman leader Selim I captured two of his wives and his entire harem, and married one of the wives to an Ottoman judge. When Ismail sent four envoys with gifts and words of praise to get her back, Selim cut off the messengers' noses and sent them back empty-handed. Heartbroken, Ismail resorted to drinking alcohol, withdrew from government and never again took part in a military campaign.

The Ottomans captured the Safavid capital Tabriz on 7 September 1514, pillaged it and then evacuated. They thoroughly looted the Persian imperial treasury. That week's Friday sermon in the city's mosques was delivered in Selim's name. Selim could not press on beyond Tabriz because of discontent among the janissaries.

The Persian Caucasian front flared up again in 1633, when the Georgian kingdoms of Kartli and Kakheti, under King Teimuraz, defied Safavid sovereignty. In 1634 the Shah sent Rustam Khan, a Georgian convert to Islam, to subdue them. Teimuraz was defeated but escaped to safety in Imereti.
As the Ottoman army retreated after Chaldiran, it was intensively harassed by Georgian light cavalry serving in the Safavid army. The raiders pursued the Ottoman troops deep into the Ottoman realm.
King Teimuraz, who had fled to Imereti after his defeat, did not stay in exile. He restored himself on the throne of Kakheti in 1638. He even won Persian recognition of this fact.

literature.text: Karacaoğlan was a 17th-century Anatolian Turkish folk poet and ashik, widely accepted to have been born around 1606 and to have died around 1679. His poems drew on nature, love, longing for home, and death. His language was expressive, yet unadorned, direct, and simple.

Beginning in the early 16th century, Persian traditions had a large impact on the Georgian ruling elites. This resulted in Persian influence on Georgian art, architecture, and literature. That cultural influence lasted until the arrival of the Russians.

Karacaoğlan's poetry gave a vivid picture of nature and village life in Anatolian settlements, in contrast to the poetry of the Ottoman palace. After the Republic of Turkey was founded in 1923, this kind of folk poetry was emphasized and became an important influence on modern lyric poetry. Karacaoğlan is regarded as its foremost exponent.

Middle Ottoman Turkish, also called Classical Ottoman Turkish, was the language of poetry and administration from the 16th century until the Tanzimat. It was largely unintelligible to rural Turks, who continued to use kaba Türkçe, a plainer speech with far fewer foreign loanwords.

The most common poetic forms of the Ottoman court came from the Persian tradition, namely the gazel and the mesnevî, or indirectly through Persian from Arabic, namely the kasîde. This style of writing came to be known as Divan literature, because divân was the Ottoman Turkish word for a poet's collected works.

Georgian writers of the Safavid era produced epics and laments about their life under the Safavid Empire. Documents in both Georgian and Persian were produced by the Bagrationi dynasty, who were subject to Iranian rulership. These writers made considerable contributions to Georgian literature.

Karacaoğlan was only a pseudonym, and his real name is thought to be Simayil, İsmail, Halil or Hasan. The Barak tribe of Gaziantep and the Çavuşlu tribe of Kilis both claim him as their own. Most people believe he was born near Çukurova and lived among Turkish tribes in the mountains of southern Anatolia.

In 1720 Mehmed Efendi was sent to Paris as Ottoman ambassador to Louis XV. During 1721–22 he toured France on a fact-finding mission to gather information for modernizing the Ottoman Empire. On his return he presented his observations to the Sultan in the form of a book, a Sefâretnâme.
Teimuraz I ruled the Kingdom of Kakheti from 1605 to 1648 under Iranian hegemony. He wrote a number of stories and historical narrations with significant Persian literary influences.

According to Hodja Hamdi Efendi of Akşehir, Karacaoğlan was an orphan who left town at an early age. Some of his poetry indicates that he took two of his sisters all the way to Bursa or Istanbul. He spent most of his life in Çukurova and Maraş.

science.text: The Ottomans used an early firearm called the tüfenk, a matchlock musket that stayed in service from the mid-15th to the late 17th century. The Janissaries had received arquebuses as early as the reign of Murad II, but most of them did not have them until the mid-16th century.

From the late 16th century the Ottomans produced flintlock muskets with a miquelet lock and gradually introduced them. Because the Ottomans were early adopters, this mechanism spread throughout the Mediterranean and the Balkans.
Janissary arquebuses are known to have played a decisive role in the Battle of Mohács in 1526. By then the weapon had been part of the Janissaries' armament for generations.

Early flintlock muskets were less reliable than matchlocks and considerably more expensive. So the Ottomans, like Western Europeans, used muskets of both systems side by side until the late 17th century, after 1688.

Technological historians credit the Ottomans with perfecting the serpentine mechanism. Yet it is not known whether the earliest Ottoman arquebuses, listed in Balkan fortress armament lists in the mid-15th century, had a serpentine lock or a more advanced matchlock.

Venetian sources state that Bayezid II supplied the Janissaries with better firearms, certainly a more modern version of the matchlock. They do not say whether the new weapon was imported from Europe or produced by the Ottomans themselves.

European sources from the 16th century often said Ottoman muskets were larger and heavier than Christian ones, but this generalization needs caution. Janissaries also used smaller, lighter muskets on a large scale, usually 115 to 140 cm long and weighing 3 to 4.5 kg, close to European matchlocks of 120 to 150 cm.
In 1567 the Janissaries in the Belgrade Fortress used muskets that fired 12- and 15-gram bullets. Muskets made in state workshops and used in Baghdad in 1571 fired 15-gram bullets.

From the weight of the lead bullets, historians estimate the Baghdad and Belgrade muskets had a caliber of between 13 and 14 mm. Smaller Janissary field muskets came in calibers of 11, 13, 14 or 16 mm, and rarely 19 or 20 mm.

politics.text: In the Ottoman Empire, a millet was an independent court of law for personal matters. Non-Muslim communities organized around their faith were allowed to rule themselves under their own laws, such as Christian canon law or Jewish halakha, but only in cases not involving any Muslim. Any dispute involving a Muslim fell under sharia-based law. Ottoman law also regarded non-Muslims as inferior subjects, denied them certain rights, excluded them from parts of the government and military, and made them pay extra taxes, such as the military-exemption tax.

Conquests by Selim I led the Ottoman sultans to adopt the title of caliph. The rulers of an empire centred in Anatolia thus added a claim to religious leadership to their political rule. The empire also granted its many confessional communities autonomy to manage their own affairs.

The Ottomans and the Safavids were arch rivals, divided by religion as well as politics. The Ottomans were staunchly Sunni and the Safavids were Shia. For centuries the two empires competed for control over eastern Anatolia, the Caucasus and Ottoman Iraq.
Suleiman the Magnificent ruled from 1520 to 1566. In his reign the Ottoman Empire became a global power. Under him the Ottomans captured Belgrade in 1521 and won the Battle of Mohács in 1526.

Historians once called the 17th century a period of Ottoman decline. Since the 1980s they have increasingly rejected that view and describe it as a period of crisis, adaptation and transformation. In this period the empire shifted from an expansionist, patrimonial state into a bureaucratic empire that stressed upholding justice and protecting Sunni Islam.

The Orthodox Christians of the empire belonged to the Rum Millet, or 'Roman nation'. Greeks, Bulgarians, Albanians, Georgians, Serbs and others were all counted in the same millet despite differences in ethnicity and language. Its religious hierarchy was dominated by the Greeks.

Heads of millets, called milletbaşı or ethnarchs, usually held absolute secular and ecclesiastical power over their communities. They answered only to the Sultan. Religious and worldly authority were thus combined in one leader within each community.

The Treaty of Zuhab of 1639 is usually considered the most significant treaty between the Ottomans and Persia. It fixed the present Turkey–Iran and Iraq–Iran borders. Later treaties frequently referred back to it.

Murad IV reigned from 1623 to 1640 and reasserted central authority during his brief majority reign. He recaptured Iraq from the Safavids in 1639. The Treaty of Zuhab of that year divided the Caucasus between the two empires as it had already been defined in the 1555 Peace of Amasya.

In the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1578 to 1590, the Ottomans conquered Georgia, Azerbaijan and western Iran. This brought the empire to its greatest territorial expansion under Murad III. The Safavids took advantage of Ottoman distraction in the west and reversed all these gains in the war of 1603 to 1618.

The Ecumenical Patriarch was recognized as the highest religious and political leader of all Eastern Orthodox subjects of the Sultan. Yet under the 1774 Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, Russia claimed rights of protection over the empire's Orthodox subjects. Religious leadership thus became entangled with great-power rivalry.

Although often called a 'system', the millets before the nineteenth century were not organized systematically. Non-Muslims simply had significant autonomy within their own communities. The notion of distinct millets for different religious communities only emerged in the eighteenth century, and later foundation myths tied it back to Mehmed the Conqueror, though no such system existed in the fifteenth century.

In May 1622 the imperial army revolted and, two days later, with the approval of the Şeyhülislâm, executed Osman II. Abaza Mehmed Pasha, governor of Erzurum, then rose in revolt, vowed revenge on the sultan's killers and massacred the janissaries wherever he found them. In the turmoil that followed, the Safavids seized Baghdad and much of Iraq in 1623. They held it until 1638, after which the border of the 1555 Treaty of Amasya was re-established.

About a fifth of the population of Constantinople in the 16th and 17th centuries consisted of slaves. Historians Halil İnalcık and Dariusz Kołodziejczyk tentatively estimated that 2 million enslaved people of Rus, Pole and Ukrainian extraction, captured in Tatar raids, entered the empire between 1500 and 1700. Other historians, such as Alan Fisher, argue that this cannot be calculated accurately.

The Ottoman provincial system was headed by governors called beylerbeys, appointed by the central government. The Beylerbey of Rumelia had the right to sit on the Imperial Council from 1536. Before 1650, some beylerbeys began to be appointed with the rank of vizier, giving them command over the governors of adjoining eyalets.

politics.text: A buyruldu, or decree, of 1793 required Ottoman Navy ships to use a red flag with a white star and crescent. Earlier war flags of the 16th and 17th centuries often showed the bifurcated Zulfiqar sword, which Western writers often misread as a pair of scissors. A version of the 1793 flag with a five-pointed star became the national flag in 1844.

culture.text: The Ottoman Empire had substantial subject populations of Orthodox subjects, Armenians, Jews and Assyrians. They were allowed a certain amount of autonomy under the millet system, and their distinctive cultures were adopted and adapted by the Ottoman state.

Armenian merchants sat at the crossroads of Central Asia, India, China and the Mediterranean. Between the 16th and 18th centuries they played a highly active and potentially dominant role in overland trade across Asia. They also established colonies in urban centers across Europe and Asia.

Famines and shortages struck Anatolia several times between 1564 and 1586, and the Little Ice Age hurt farming in eastern Anatolia. A drought in eastern Anatolia in 1599 produced a famine in 1600, and another famine followed in 1607 to 1608. Arakel of Tabriz wrote about allegations of cannibalism during that later famine, meaning people were said to have eaten human flesh to survive.

In 1545, Shah Tahmasp I issued a farman making the city of Julfa a waqf of the nearby St. Stephen's Monastery. Julfa enjoyed the privileged status of a crown domain, so its citizens paid taxes directly to the royal treasury. This protected Julfans from the arbitrary interference of regular state tax collectors.

David, the Armenian Patriarch of Jerusalem from 1583 to 1615, acquired a debt of 40,000 kuruş. Pilgrims, his main source of revenue, stopped coming to Jerusalem because of Celali raids. Grigor Daranaḷts‘i noted that the financial situation improved by 1616.
